title: Bias-variance tradeoff: the framework behind under- and overfitting
intro: Under- and overfitting are not two separate ailments but two ends of one trade-off: simplicity (bias) versus sensitivity (variance). This topic explains the mathematical decomposition, lets you drag the U-curve yourself, and actually measures bias and variance in a simulation.
keyPoints: A model's expected error decomposes into three sources: bias² (systematically off), variance (fickle across training sets) and irreducible noise σ².
Underfitting = high bias (train and test both poor); overfitting = high variance (train perfect, test poor).
The total error is a U-curve in model complexity: too simple on the left, too fickle on the right, and the optimum sits exactly in the valley.
Every knob shifts the balance: max_depth, C, regularisation, k in kNN, more data — and ensembles average variance away.

blocks.html: Why does your model make mistakes? The bias-variance decomposition splits the expected error into three independent sources. Fix a point \( x \), a true function \( f \), and a model \( \hat{f} \) trained on a random training set (so \( \hat{f} \) is itself a random variable — different training set, different fit). Then:

blocks.label: bias-variance decomposition
blocks.caption: The expected squared error at a point, taken over all possible training sets. Bias measures the systematic deviation, variance the spread between fits, σ² the noise in the data itself.

blocks.html: Bias is the systematic error: averaged over all possible training sets the prediction is off — the model simply does not understand the pattern (a straight line through a sine stays wrong everywhere). Variance is the fickleness: how much the prediction changes when you merely swap the training set. A model with many degrees of freedom can bend towards every training set — handy for hiding training error, disastrous when the training set contains noise. Irreducible noise \( \sigma^2 \) finally lives in the data itself (measurement errors, hidden factors) and no model can remove it — the floor under your error.

rows: is my model on average off target?
systematic, repeats on every training set
how much does the fit change across training sets?
how much noise is in the data itself?
cannot be lowered — the absolute floor

blocks.html: The classic analogy: an archer on a target. Bias is where the group sits on average (far from the bullseye = high bias); variance is how far apart the shots scatter (widely spread = high variance). Irreducible noise is the wind, which every archer must reckon with. A good archer shoots a tight group in the centre: low bias and low variance.

In the topic The ML workflow you saw under- and overfitting as train/test curves. The decomposition now gives them a precise meaning. A model with high bias is too simple for the pattern: it scores poorly on train and test, with the two scores close together — adding capacity helps (more features, a deeper tree, less regularisation). A model with high variance is too sensitive: the train score is (nearly) perfect, the test score collapses — the gap between the two is the diagnosis.

rows: poor train, poor test, small gap
more complexity, more features, higher C, deeper
perfect train, poor test, large gap

blocks.html: Examples of the bias-variance dialogue on this site: C in logistic regression and SVMs (Regularisation) shrinks coefficients — bias up, variance down; max_depth in trees (Decision trees) does exactly the same via the depth of the step function (Regression trees); and the choice of k in k-fold cross-validation shifts the bias/variance of the estimate itself.

sections.title: The U-curve: complexity shifts the balance

blocks.html: Put model complexity on the horizontal axis and the three error sources on the vertical. Bias² falls: more complexity means more capacity to capture the pattern. Variance rises: more degrees of freedom means more room to absorb noise. The sum — plus the fixed noise floor — is a U-curve with an optimum in the valley. Drag the slider and hunt for the minimum:

blocks.title: The bias-variance U-curve
blocks.subtitle: Drag the complexity slider from the left (too simple, bias dominates) to the right (too fickle, variance dominates) — the total error is optimal only in the valley (c ≈ 4.8), where it lights up green.
blocks.xlabel: model complexity (e.g. tree depth, polynomial degree)

blocks.html: Two footnotes to this canonical picture. First, the axis is ordinal, not a physical unit: “complexity” is whatever your model scales — tree depth, polynomial degree, parameter count, 1/C. Second, the valley is broader than the curve suggests: in practice you may sit on the left of the optimum, because a slightly too simple model is robust, interpretable and often generalises better than the exact optimum in your single split. “Rather too simple than exactly right” is a healthy working attitude, not laziness.

The curve also explains why more data lowers variance but not bias: with larger training sets the fickleness of the fit averages out (the yellow curve drops), but a wrong model stays systematically off (the cyan curve does not move). If your model has high bias, more data will not help — the model itself must change.
Everything you have seen in this course in hyperparameters and design choices is ultimately a bias-variance knob. The overview:

rows: — (not a knob, still the best medicine)
out of scope — but now understandable

blocks.html: The knobs are not independent: more data plus a larger model can work out better than either alone; regularisation works poorly on unscaled features (see Regularisation); and an ensemble of underfitted trees only averages away the variance — the bias remains. Treat the table as a map, not an autopilot: the final call always rests on measured validation scores.

sections.title: Actually measuring bias and variance: the simulation

blocks.html: The decomposition sounds abstract, but you can compute it literally: generate many training sets from the same true function, fit a model on each, and inspect the spread of predictions per point. Below: the truth is \( \sin(2\pi x) \) with noise, and we predict at \( x = 0{,}25 \) (the peak) with polynomials of degree 1, 3 and 9 — 200 times on freshly random training sets:

blocks.caption: measuring the bias-variance decomposition with NumPy
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
f = lambda x: np.sin(2 * np.pi * x)   # true function
x_eval, truth = 0.25, f(0.25)          # measurement point: the peak

degrees = (1, 3, 9)
preds = {g: [] for g in degrees}
for _ in range(200):                  # 200 random training sets
    x = rng.uniform(0, 1, 25)
    y = f(x) + rng.normal(0, 0.35, 25)
    for g in degrees:
        c = np.polyfit(x, y, g)
        preds[g].append(np.polyval(c, x_eval))

print('truth f(0.25) =', round(truth, 3))
print()
print('degree |    bias   | variance | bias2+var')
for g in degrees:
    v = np.array(preds[g])
    b = v.mean() - truth
    print(f'{g:6d} | {b:9.3f} | {v.var():9.3f} | {b**2 + v.var():10.3f}')

blocks.html: Read the table as the three archers. Degree 1: the straight line cannot reach the peak — sizeable bias, small variance (every line resembles every other). Degree 9: nine degrees of freedom — the fit whips along with the noise of every training set and the predictions at \( x = 0{,}25 \) scatter in all directions: bias near zero, variance large. Degree 3 captures the bend without chasing the noise: the smallest sum. That is the U-curve from the interactive plot, now with real numbers.

Try setting x_eval to 0.5 (where the truth is 0) or raising the noise from 0.35 to 0.7 and re-running the cell: high noise mainly inflates the variance of the flexible models, while the bias of degree 1 stays untouched. Simulations like these are the cheapest way to build bias-variance intuition — you watch the mathematics move.

In reality you do not know the true function, so you cannot measure bias and variance directly. What you do have is the proxy from the diagnosis table: train versus validation/test score, and the most robust way to determine it is cross-validation (see Cross-validation). The code below scans max_depth for the breast-cancer dataset and lets the U-curve appear in the output:

blocks.caption: finding the max_depth optimum with cross-validation
blocks.source:
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
print('max_depth | mean CV accuracy (5-fold)')
for d in (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, None):
    tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d, random_state=0)
    scores = cross_val_score(tree, X, y, cv=5)
    print(f'{str(d):9s} | {scores.mean():.3f}')

blocks.html: The typical picture here: accuracy jumps between depth 1 and 2 (0.900 → 0.928) and then slides back slightly towards 0.916 — deeper trees buy no extra generalisation, only more degrees of freedom. Note: this is the practical version of the U-curve — less smooth than the idealised picture, because every score itself carries noise (more on that below). In production you pick, from the plateau, preferably the simplest model: same score, fewer degrees of freedom, better interpretability.

Do not mix up these terms: the bias/variance of your model (this topic) is about generalising to new data; the bias/variance of the CV estimate (in Cross-validation) is about how accurately your measurement of generalisation approximates the truth. Both are called a trade-off, but they are different sliders: the first you tune with hyperparameters, the second with the choice of k.

The big picture in one breath: underfitting is bias, overfitting is variance, and everything you tune moves you along the U-curve. Trees are the illustrative example — max_depth is the bias-variance knob in its purest form — while regularisation, kernels and even the choice of k follow the same track. Once you know this decomposition, you never look at a train-test gap the same way again.
